intro: DAU/MAU Stickiness measures how much of your monthly active base shows up on a typical day. Enter average daily active users and monthly active users to get the rate.

sections.heading: How DAU/MAU Stickiness is calculated
sections.body: Stickiness = Average Daily Active Users ÷ Monthly Active Users — [the same DAU-over-MAU shape MetricHQ uses to define the ratio](https://www.metrichq.org/saas/dau-mau-ratio/). Every daily active user is, by definition, also part of that same month's active user count, so DAU is always a subset of MAU for the same window — the ratio can approach 100% as engagement gets more consistent, but it can't legitimately exceed it.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: 20,000 ÷ 100,000 = 20.00%. On a typical day, a fifth of everyone who was active at some point that month showed up — a read on how concentrated engagement is within the monthly base, not on how many people are active in total.

sections.heading: A proxy for habit, not proof of it
sections.body: Stickiness is commonly described as a proxy for habit formation — a higher ratio means a larger share of the monthly base is showing up daily, which is consistent with a habitual usage pattern. It only describes users who are already active at all, though; whether new users reach that point in the first place is what [Activation Rate](/calculators/activation-rate) measures instead. The ratio itself only counts whether someone was active on a given day; it has no visibility into why. A messaging app and a once-a-week grocery-delivery app can be equally well-loved by their users while posting very different stickiness numbers, simply because daily use makes sense for one and not the other. A change in stickiness is worth investigating, but the number alone doesn't say whether users are forming a habit or just being counted by a definition of "active" that happens to fit daily use.

sections.heading: Stickiness vs. Day-N Retention
sections.body: Both are mobile-growth staples, but they measure fundamentally different things. Stickiness is a rolling snapshot across the whole active base — on any given day, what fraction of this month's users are showing up, independent of when any individual user first joined. [Day-N Retention](/calculators/d1-retention) instead follows one specific signup cohort forward to a chosen day and checks what share came back. A product can have strong stickiness overall while a specific recent cohort's D1 retention looks weak, since stickiness blends together users who joined at very different times, and Day-N retention deliberately isolates just one cohort's age-since-signup behavior.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
items: Treating a change in stickiness as proof users are forming or breaking a habit. The ratio counts whether someone was active on a given day, not why — it's a proxy, not direct evidence of habitual behavior.

Comparing stickiness across product categories without accounting for expected use frequency. A daily-habit product (messaging, social feeds) and a weekly or monthly-use product (bill pay, grocery delivery) will post very different stickiness numbers even when both are performing well for their category.
Using inconsistent activity definitions between DAU and MAU. If "active" means something different in the daily count than in the monthly count, the ratio no longer describes what it's supposed to.

Reading DAU as if it could exceed MAU. Since every daily active user by definition also counts toward that month's active users, a DAU higher than MAU signals a data or window-alignment problem, not a real result.

faq.a: DAU/MAU Stickiness measures how much of a product's monthly active user base shows up on a typical day, calculated as average daily active users divided by monthly active users. A stickiness of 20% means that on an average day, a fifth of everyone active at some point that month was active that specific day. Since every daily active user is, by definition, part of that same month's active count, DAU can never exceed MAU for the same window — the ratio is naturally capped at 100%, and higher values indicate more concentrated, frequent engagement within the monthly base rather than more total users overall.

faq.q: How do you calculate DAU/MAU Stickiness?
faq.a: Divide average daily active users by monthly active users: Stickiness = DAU ÷ MAU. A product with 20,000 average daily active users and 100,000 monthly active users has a stickiness of 20,000 ÷ 100,000 = 20.00%. Both figures need to use the same definition of "active" (the same qualifying action) and cover the same time window — mixing a daily count built on one activity definition with a monthly count built on another produces a ratio that doesn't describe real user behavior. Most product analytics platforms calculate and report this automatically once an "active" event is defined, so it rarely needs to be computed by hand.

faq.q: Does high stickiness prove users have formed a habit?
faq.a: Not on its own. Stickiness is commonly described as a proxy for habit formation, since a higher ratio does mean more of the monthly base is returning daily. But the metric only counts whether a qualifying activity happened on a given day — it has no way to distinguish a genuine habit from any other reason someone happened to show up. It also can't account for products where daily use isn't the natural pattern in the first place: a weekly-use product can be performing excellently for its category while posting a stickiness number that would look weak for a messaging app.

faq.q: Can DAU be higher than MAU?
faq.a: No, not in a correctly measured result. Every user counted as active on a given day is, by the definitions involved, also active at some point during that same month, so DAU is always a subset of MAU covering the same window. If a calculation shows DAU higher than MAU, that's a signal of a data problem — most commonly a mismatch in what counts as "active" between the two counts, or the daily and monthly windows not actually aligning to the same period — rather than a legitimate result the formula can produce. This calculator treats that state as invalid input, not a valid edge case.

faq.q: How is Stickiness different from Day-N Retention?
faq.a: Stickiness is a rolling, whole-base snapshot: on any given day, what share of the month's active users showed up, with no connection to when any individual user first signed up. Day-N Retention instead follows one specific signup cohort forward and checks what share returned on a chosen day after joining. A product can post strong overall stickiness from a large, engaged existing base while a specific recent cohort's Day-N retention looks weak, since stickiness blends users of every tenure together and Day-N retention isolates just one cohort's age-since-signup behavior on its own, with no reference to the wider active base at all.
